article.plain_text:
Astra is OpenAI's name for its frontier GPT-6.2 model. What shipped on November 17 is a pair:
GPT-6.2 Astra, for hard projects
GPT-6.2 Sol, for everyday work
The same day, at Microsoft Ignite, Satya Nadella said GPT-6.2 is coming to Foundry and "sets a new bar for AI in professional work." Both Astra and Sol are generally available there now.
I work at Microsoft. Everything below is public information. These views are my own.
The real comparison
Builders are mainly comparing four models:
GPT-6.2 Astra (OpenAI, Nov 17)
Claude Fable 5.2 (Anthropic, Nov 9)
Gemini 4 Carbon (Google, Nov 10)
Grok 4.7 (xAI, Sept 21)
The cheaper everyday lane is GPT-6.2 Sol, plus Google's Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which launched on November 12.
Price per 1M tokens (input / outpu
GPT-6.2 Astra: $8 / $40, 1.05M context
Claude Fable 5.2: $8 / $40, 1M context
Gemini 4 Carbon: $2 / $10 until Nov 30, then $4 / $20, 1M context
Grok 4.7: $2 / $6 (under 200K prompts), 500K context
GPT-6.2 Sol: $2 / $10
Gemini 4 Hydrogen: $1.50 / $7.50
What the numbers actually say
On Artificial Analysis's independent Intelligence Index, Claude Fable 5.2 (Max) scores 65 and GPT-6.2 Astra (Max) scores 62.
OpenAI says Astra beats Fable 5.2 by 5.5 points on Agents' Last Exam, at a much lower cost per task. That's OpenAI's own test.
Google says Carbon ranks #1 on CursorBench 4.0 at more than 2x lower cost per task. That's Google's own claim.
Anthropic's Nov 9 table had Fable ahead on FrontierCode 2.0, but against the older GPT-6 Astra.
Every vendor's chart says they win. I'm not going to invent a single winner.
For vibe coders
If you're shipping small apps, start with Sol or Hydrogen. They're built for coding agents and daily work.
Reach for Astra, Fable, or Carbon on long jobs: a messy repo, a strict template, or an agent that has to plan and use tools for a while.
Early reactions on X are mixed and only hours old. Some testers say Astra is much cheaper and faster than Fable, but not at the same quality. Others still prefer Opus 5.5 for daily coding.
Which one should you use?
Daily vibe coding: GPT-6.2 Sol or Gemini 4 Hydrogen
Hardest long-horizon work: try Astra and Fable 5.2 on your own repo, and keep the one that survives
Multimodal and Google tools: Gemini 4 Carbon
Already in Cursor or the Grok API: Grok 4.7 is still in the mix, but wait for fresh tests
Price per token isn't the whole story. Cost per task is. A cheap model that retries five times can lose to a pricier one that finishes once.
The field moved twice in eight days. The only ranking that matters is the one on your project.
Which model are you trying first, and on what? 👇

note_tweet.text:
The benchmark wars just changed shape. Artificial Analysis has released Intelligence Index v5 — its biggest methodology overhaul since January — and the headline isn't which model won. It's that the ground itself moved: 60% of the Index now runs on private test sets or held-out answers, making contamination — the quiet scandal of the LLM benchmark era — structurally much harder to pull off.

The scores: Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads at 58, ahead of GPT-6 Astra (max) at 57 and GPT-6.1 Sol (max) at 55. Anthropic and OpenAI hold the entire top five between them. Google's Gemini 4 Argon (high) sits next at 50. No single model sweeps the board — v5 splits the Index evenly across four domains at 25% each: Knowledge Work, Coding, Science, and General.

Three findings matter more than the ranking itself.

1. The open-weights gap just widened from 3 points to 12. Kimi K3.1 Pro tops the open-weights table at 46 — but its weights aren't released yet. Among models you can actually download and run, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 (max) and GLM-5.3 (max) lead at 32 — a full 26 points behind the leader, and below even Claude Haiku 5.5 (max) at 36. If you're betting on open weights closing the frontier gap this year, this is the chart that says: not yet.

2. Cost per task varies by more than 13x among the leading models. Of the ten highest scorers, GPT-6.1 Terra (max) delivers an Intelligence Index task for $0.96, while Claude Fable 5.1 (max) costs $13.04 for the same unit of work. Same leaderboard, radically different economics. Procurement teams should read the price column before the score column.

3. The new benchmarks are agentic and practical. FrontierCode 2.0 — Cognition's private benchmark launched the same day — comprises 132 tasks in real open-source repositories, graded on whether a repository maintainer would actually merge the agent's change. Fail any blocking check and you score zero. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) leads it at 46%, with GPT-6 Astra, GPT-6.1 Terra and Claude Sonnet 5.5 all at 42%. The best open-weights performer, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, manages 28% — 18 points back. Terminal-Bench-Science adds 70 expert-curated scientific research tasks run in a live terminal, where every test must pass for credit.

There's also a new Progress Index v1, placing every model since November 2022 on one continuous capability scale — built, they note, on learnings from Epoch AI's Capabilities Index. It's the right split: Progress Index for capability over time, Intelligence Index for the current frontier.

The deeper story: evaluation is finally growing teeth. Public benchmarks saturate, leak into training data, and get gamed. Private held-out sets, merge-or-fail coding grades, and per-task cost accounting are what measurement looks like when a technology stops being a demo and becomes infrastructure. And the 23-point swing that reasoning effort alone can produce is a reminder that "which model is smartest" is increasingly the wrong question — the right one is "which model, at which effort level, at what cost, for which task."

The frontier is razor-thin at the top — one point between first and second. The gap that's widening is everywhere else.

Today @OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. 

I'm sure dropping this right before Anthropic's IPO is just a coincidence :) 

Yes, the models are smarter, better and faster.  What was also impressive is that it's also cheaper. OpenAI says GPT-6.2 Astra scored 5.2 points higher than GPT-6 Astra on Agents’ Last Exam, a test of multistep professional work, while costing less than one-third as much to run on that test.

For anyone trying to put AI to work across a company, that’s a meaningful change in the economics. 

Astra is also getting better at work people actually hand to a colleague. 

Give it source files and a template, and it can build a valuation workbook, draft an investment memo or prepare a quarterly review in the format your team uses. 

OpenAI released Sol alongside it for everyday work. I think that pairing matters. A finance team might use Astra to work through a difficult valuation and Sol for the weekly reporting that follows. https://t.co/XClMjduWw2

Put that alongside what’s happened across the industry in the first 17 days of November.

➡️ @spacexai Super Intelligence followed Grok 4.7, its model for coding and knowledge work, with Grok Bot 1.0 on November 2. A team can bring the bot into Slack or Teams, have it join a meeting and follow up on unfinished work. That’s a product employees can delegate to today.

➡️ @Anthropic released Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 on November 9. They share an underlying model. Fable is broadly available, while access to Mythos is restricted to vetted organizations working in cybersecurity and biomedical research. Anthropic says its engineers used the models on software migrations they previously considered infeasible.

➡️ @Meta released Muse Ember that same day. Its smallest model is designed for tasks an agent may repeat hundreds of times in one session, like reading files or running tests. At that volume, the cost of each step matters.

➡️ @Google broadened access to Gemini 4 Carbon, the successor to Argon, on November 10. Two days later it released Gemini 4 Hydrogen. Google is already previewing how to use them together, with a stronger model coordinating a project and faster models handling parts of the work. 

So much for "pacing the frontier"...there's really no slowing down on the exponential intelligence curve we’re on. 

A more capable model makes a new assignment possible. A cheaper model makes it affordable to repeat. Put both inside the software people already use and a team can start delegating work that, a quarter ago, it still had to do by hand.

As we prepare for 2027, it's time for directors and executives to revisit the assumptions in their annual operating plans about what still takes a week or a month to accomplish, what still costs too much to do and where an experienced person needs to make a judgement call.

Welcome to the agentic enterprise...and we're just getting started.

#AgenticEnterprise
#OpenAI

note_tweet.text:
AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI regularly publish reports on how people are using products like Claude and ChatGPT, but they only release the data they want us to see, AI researchers say. 

“There is no independent source to corroborate it,” says Anka Reuel, a computer science PhD candidate at the Stanford Trustworthy AI Research (STAIR) Lab. 

Reuel is co-lead of a new research project, called the AI Observatory, that aims to fill the gap. It’s a public platform that aggregated and analyzed real AI conversations with popular models like Claude and Gemini that were collected with users’ consent through seven existing datasets. The intent is to provide independent sources of information that can help researchers and policymakers assess how people are using generative AI. Highly consequential decisions about AI’s benefits and risks are currently being made on the basis of very limited data, says Reuel. 

The AI Observatory found that AI use differs significantly across models and has changed over time. Its research shows many more sensitive behaviors than are captured in reports from major AI companies, which they say focus more on work than on personal use. 

The Anthropic Economic Index is one of the best-known and most widely cited sources of AI usage data, but it has blind spots. As its name suggests, it focuses on work- and productivity-related uses of Claude AI—filtering out conversations that are unrelated to these uses. 

When the AI Observatory researchers applied Anthropic’s methods to their dataset, they found that nearly half the conversations—48%—would have been filtered out. Those non-work-related conversations were more likely to involve health and relationships (44.2% versus 31.2% in Anthropic’s analysis), adult or illicit topics (7.9% versus 2.1%), harassment and hate (27.5% versus 5.66%), and sexual content (16.7% versus 2.4%). (OpenAI’s 2025 report on ChatGPT, similarly, found that only 30% of consumer use was related to work.)

Anthropic has released separate blog posts on how people use Claude for support or companionship, and even to generate CSAM, but “having [the AI Observatory’s] bird’s-eye-view analysis” rather than leaving that information “sectioned off into a separate report” helps researchers understand the different uses more consistently, says David Widder, an assistant professor at the University of Texas at Austin, who researches how people interact with AI systems and is not involved with the AI Observatory. 

The datasets the AI Observatory looked at include conversations that took place between 2023 and 2025, and it found differences both in how people were using AI and how various AI platforms responded. 

Conversations within WildChat, one of the largest and most detailed datasets included in the AI Observatory’s study, got longer and more elaborate over time, as indicated by growing numbers of prompt tokens, response tokens, and conversation turns. 

There was also significantly more small talk over time. That suggests that AI companionship was increasing; meanwhile, the AI assistants’ self-disclosure (i.e., admitting to being a chatbot) decreased. 

Additionally, exchanges that the researchers labeled as sensitive—meaning ones with potentially harmful or restricted content, including sexual harassment and hate speech—became less frequent. That might suggest that platforms were generally deploying more effective safeguards. 

The AI Observatory also found that topics, interaction styles, conversation structures, and the likelihood and type of sensitive use cases differed from one model to another. 

For example, the researchers found that people used Grok and Gemini more frequently for information retrieval. Grok, in particular, was especially popular for information on news and politics, but it was also where misinformation tended to concentrate. (This is consistent with other research that has shown how readily misinformation proliferates on Grok. xAI did not respond to a request for comment.) 

Meanwhile, people were more likely to turn to Anthropic for coding, Gemini for social and roleplay uses, and ChatGPT for homework assistance. 

There were even differences between different versions of the same model. Researchers found that people had shorter conversations with ChatGPT when it was powered by GPT-3.5, and longer and more iterative ones with GPT-4o—which makes sense given that that version became known for leading to emotional addiction. 

Companies’ reports, however, didn’t tend to capture these nuances between or even within their own models. “No single company report tells the whole story,” says Shayne Longpre, a recent PhD graduate from the MIT Media Lab who co-led the research with Reuel. 

To create the AI Observatory, Reuel and researchers from MIT, Stanford, the Data Provenance Initiative, and other institutions aggregated 85,633 conversational turns (that is, the user prompt and corresponding AI response) across 24,521 conversations from seven real-world datasets collected in previous research. These conversations came from 5,000 users interacting with 52 different models, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, and Grok, between 2023 and 2025. 

But these conversations are a drop in the proverbial bucket compared with the data that the big labs themselves have access to. The latest Anthropic Economic AI Index, for example, is based on analysis of 1 million Claude conversations; OpenAI’s report on how people are using ChatGPT analyzed 1.5 million conversations.  

An Anthropic representative said the company’s published research reflects its research teams’ specific questions and interests and that it’s important to support external independent research. OpenAI did not respond to requests for comment. 

The fact that the AI Observatory’s dataset draws from voluntarily provided sources means it’s probably underrepresenting sensitive uses, which people may be less likely to share. Thus, the researchers caution that its findings are not indicative of all AI use. 

The project’s work, though, broadens access for the research community. AI companies don’t typically share their chat data for analysis, which means their reports tend to focus on the findings that paint them in the best light, independent researchers like Reuel and Widder say. 

“When we want to ask, for example: is Anthropic’s general-purpose AI system … used mostly for good or mostly for bad … we don’t have a way of answering that question because that information is proprietary,” explains Widder.

The AI Observatory’s data will be available to researchers for analysis, and the team hopes to expand its datasets over time. Ideally, Reuel says, the AI companies would share their data with independent researchers—in ways that protect user privacy, of course. But as it currently stands, she says, anyone making decisions based on AI usage data risks “completely operating in the wild and making these really consequential decisions without knowing what’s actually happening beyond those company narratives.”

article.plain_text:
Every lab sells an effort dial now. Low, medium, high, xhigh, max. Turn it up and the model thinks longer, and you pay for every thinking token.

The pitch is simple: more effort, more intelligence. Nobody puts the exchange rate on the pricing page. So I worked it out.

THE METHOD

Artificial Analysis runs every model through its Intelligence Index v5 and publishes two numbers per effort setting: the score, and the cost per Index task (tokens actually used, at list price). For 11 models with an effort ladder, I took the top setting and the one right below it, then divided the extra cost by the extra score.

That gives dollars per extra point, per task. It's the price of the last notch. Lower is better.

Every list price below was checked on the vendor's own pricing page today. AA also publishes time per task, so you get the latency bill too.

THE TABLE (worst last notch first)

1. Grok 4.7 (High→Xhigh): 35.2 → 35.5 pts (+0.27), $6.18 → $7.77/task (1.26x), $5.82 per extra point, 21 → 25 min/task
2. Claude Fable 5.2 (Xhigh→Max): 62.2 → 64.6 pts (+2.35), $14.83 → $26.54/task (1.79x), $4.99 per extra point, 26 → 41 min/task
3. Claude Opus 5.5 (Xhigh→Max): 57.4 → 59.1 pts (+1.66), $6.05 → $10.04/task (1.66x), $2.40 per extra point, 16 → 25 min/task
4. GPT-6 Astra (Xhigh→Max): 55.3 → 56.9 pts (+1.55), $3.66 → $6.24/task (1.71x), $1.67 per extra point, 11 → 20 min/task
5. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (Xhigh→Max): 49.9 → 54.5 pts (+4.62), $4.09 → $10.02/task (2.45x), $1.28 per extra point, 14 → 32 min/task
6. Muse Wonder (High→Max): 40.5 → 43.6 pts (+3.05), $4.56 → $6.95/task (1.52x), $0.78 per extra point, 9 → 13 min/task
7. Gemini 4 Carbon (Medium→High): 58.3 → 60.0 pts (+1.77), $4.68 → $5.48/task (1.17x), $0.46 per extra point, 30 → 31 min/task
8. Gemini 4 Hydrogen (High→Xhigh): 50.8 → 53.9 pts (+3.13), $1.87 → $3.16/task (1.69x), $0.41 per extra point, 8 → 15 min/task
9. GPT-6.1 Sol (Xhigh→Max): 52.5 → 54.6 pts (+2.15), $0.76 → $1.27/task (1.67x), $0.24 per extra point, 10 → 23 min/task
10. GPT-6.1 Terra (Xhigh→Max): 45.3 → 51.3 pts (+6.08), $0.40 → $0.96/task (2.40x), $0.09 per extra point, 6 → 14 min/task
11. Claude Haiku 5.5 (Xhigh→Max): 34.6 → 36.5 pts (+1.85), $0.25 → $0.41/task (1.65x), $0.09 per extra point, 10 → 15 min/task

$ per extra point = (cost per task at top setting − cost one notch below) ÷ (score difference). Carbon's notch is Medium→High because its Low setting costs more than Medium (see below).

LAST PLACE: GROK 4.7

Grok 4.7's top setting, Xhigh, adds 0.27 points. A quarter of a point. For that, the bill goes from $6.18 to $7.77 a task and each task takes about three minutes longer. That's $5.82 per extra point, the worst exchange rate on the board.

And the point you're buying is point number 35. For $7.77 a task you get 35.5. GPT-6.1 Terra at medium effort scores 38.2 for 17 cents, 2.2% of the price. Claude Haiku 5.5 at max scores 36.5 for 41 cents. Grok's modest token price ($2/$6) doesn't help when the model never stops thinking.

On AA, Grok 4.7's effort dial has three positions: fine, expensive, and decorative.

ANTHROPIC: THE SMARTEST NOTCH, AND THE DUMBEST ONE

Fable 5.2's Max setting is second worst: +2.35 points for +$11.71 a task, $4.99 per point, and each task goes from 26 to 41 minutes. One Fable Max task costs $26.54, which buys about 21 GPT-6.1 Sol Max tasks.

But the worst single notch on the entire board isn't a top setting. It's Fable going from High to Xhigh: +0.4 points for +$5.75. That's $14.56 per point. Xhigh on Fable is a 63% surcharge for a rounding error.

Sonnet 5.5 has the opposite problem. Its Max notch actually buys something (+4.6 points), but Max costs $10.02 a task and takes 32 minutes. Opus 5.5 at Xhigh scores 2.9 points more for 40% less money and half the time. If you're running Sonnet on Max, you're paying a premium to use the cheaper model.

Even better: Fable 5.2 at Low scores 53.9, basically Sonnet Max's 54.5, for $3.10. That's 31% of the price and 5 minutes instead of 32. Anthropic's best budget option is its most expensive model on its lowest setting.

GOOGLE: A SETTING THAT COSTS MORE TO BE WORSE

Gemini 4 Carbon at Low costs $5.22 a task and scores 54.2. Carbon at Medium costs $4.68 and scores 58.3. Low costs 12% more and scores 4 points less. Low isn't a budget mode. It's a setting you pay extra for to get a dumber model.

Carbon's real top notch (Medium→High) is the cheapest premium upgrade on the board: +1.77 points for 81 cents. Enjoy it for two weeks. Google's pricing page doubles every Carbon rate on December 1, so that notch goes to about 91 cents a point, assuming AA's token counts stay put.

Hydrogen's Xhigh is fairly priced at 41 cents a point, but it nearly doubles the wait, 8 to 15 minutes.

OPENAI: CHEAP NOTCHES, LONG WAITS

GPT-6.1 Terra's Max notch is the best deal here: +6.08 points for 56 cents. That's 9 cents a point, and Terra goes from 45 to 51. Sol's Max costs 24 cents a point.

The catch is time, not money. Sol Max takes 23 minutes per task versus 10 at Xhigh. OpenAI's max effort is cheap per dollar and expensive per coffee break.

THE CHEAPEST TICKET TO 50 POINTS, BY LAB

→ OpenAI: GPT-6.1 Sol High, 50.3 for $0.59 a task, 7.5 minutes.
→ Google: Gemini 4 Hydrogen High, 50.8 for $1.87.
→ Anthropic: Claude Fable 5.2 Low, 53.9 for $3.10.
→ xAI, Alibaba, Moonshot: no setting reaches 50. Best scores: Kimi K3.1 Pro 46.5, Qwen4 Max 42.9, Grok 4.7 35.5.
→ Meta: only Muse Wonder Full gets there (50.1), and it has no per-token price on Meta's API pricing page.

OpenAI sells a 50-point task for about a fifth of Anthropic's cheapest route, and xAI doesn't sell one at all.

FINE PRINT

The Index is one fixed suite. Your workload has its own token habits, and a 0.3-point gap is small enough that it could move on a re-run. AA's costs use list prices and its measured cache-hit rates. Batch and enterprise discounts change the absolute numbers. Haiku 5.5 is at its short-prompt price tier. Carbon is at today's price; its December 1 doubling is noted above as my arithmetic.

VERDICT

The effort dial is a pricing page nobody publishes. At OpenAI the last notch costs pocket change and a longer wait. At Anthropic it costs real money, and on Fable it sometimes buys nothing. On Grok 4.7 it buys a quarter of a point for $1.59.

Before you set effort to max, ask what the last notch buys. On Grok 4.7, and on Fable's Xhigh, the answer is almost nothing.

Sources: artificialanalysis.ai (Intelligence Index v5.0.1 scores, cost per Intelligence Index task and time per task by effort setting, retrieved 17 Nov 2026, 09:17 Madrid) and the official pricing pages of Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, xAI and Meta, checked the same morning.
